work_order.understanding: Issue #20 is the safety slice of epic #14 and it is greenfield. I verified independently of the proposal and the critique: there is no src/policy/, no src/executor/, no src/strategy/guardian.js, no approvals/capabilities/action_records/kill_switches/trust_ledger store anywhere under src/ or in db.js's MIGRATIONS (which end at 004_knowledge_tables, src/data/db.js:173). The approvals page today (src/web/pages.js:741-800) is a static shell: it reads raw events of type 'approval.requested' (no fixture ever writes one, so it is always empty), renders the hardcoded AUTONOMY_POSTURE constant at :734-739, and its Approve/Reject buttons at :791-792 have no listener in client.js. Nothing gates a mutation because there is no module between an ActionIntent and a provider write. I also verified two things the critique surfaced and the proposal missed: the repo already ships the atomic single-winner primitive this work needs (repositories.idempotency.claim, an INSERT OR IGNORE returning true iff this call created the claim, src/data/repositories.js:148, with a release at :158 for a failed effect), and maturityFor/policyBand are already imported by src/api/routes.js:16/19 but used only inside GET /v1/metrics (:157-158) — so the band gate has an existing, correct source of truth sitting one function away. The binding decision from the brief (and the issue body) is Meta Ads first, Google Ads later, so every write targets the Meta adapter seam. The five split criteria IAC-1..IAC-5 are each carried by one acceptance entry below.
work_order.root_cause: There is no write path to gate. The repo has no module between an ActionIntent and a provider write, so the safety contract this issue is asked for — TR-2 credential isolation, TR-3 signed capabilities, TR-4 kill switches, TR-5 nonce idempotency plus reconciliation, TR-19 per-class trust, TR-24 fail-closed writes — has no code to hold it. The approvals page cannot be more than a static shell because no approval row, receipt, capability or trust row is stored anywhere, and the autonomy posture it displays is a hardcoded array read by nothing.
work_order.approach:
Build the write path as four new modules plus one composition point, on the repo's existing patterns (additive migration, tenant-bound repositories, one pure function per rule, node:test suites mirroring src/). v5's diagnosis was right and I kept it. This revision answers the one recorded rejection by taking the reviewer's option (a) — implementing the gate — and then repairs the five places where v5's own gate was not actually the single owner it claimed to be.

ONE MINTER, ONE CHOKE POINT. The recorded rejection demanded that the trust ledger gate a write end to end, and v5 answered that correctly in principle (gate at issuance, because a capability cannot exist without passing validateIntent) but then specified the approve route with its own parallel gate, so the human-approval path — the money-moving one — skipped the micro-limit, the band and the no-evidence refusal. CORRECTED: both issuance routes (POST /v1/capabilities and POST /v1/approvals/:id/approve) call kernel.validateIntent(intent, {nowIso, trust, approval, maturity}) and nothing else may mint a capability. issueCapability takes the {ok, intent} object validateIntent returns, so a route physically cannot sign an unvalidated intent, and a static import-boundary assertion pins the only two call sites. The two routes are symmetric: the same gate, differing only in whether an approval row is supplied.

THE POSTURE LADDER, and what each rung does. monotonic, so no route can launder a class into authority:
  - shadow (or a pinned class, or one with no evidence at all) -> AUTONOMY_NOT_EARNED on BOTH issuance routes, even with a valid pending approval. Shadow means authority has not been granted yet; a human approval is not a way around it. This is the fail-closed reading of TR-19 and TR-24.
  - approval-required -> issues only when a non-terminal, unexpired approval row for the same tenant and action class is supplied. The approval row is the authority; the micro-limit still applies.
  - autonomous-under-micro-limits -> issues with NO approval row. POST /v1/capabilities is that route, and it is what makes IAC-4 observable end to end.

THE FAILURE FIXTURE MUST BE APPROVABLE (corrects v5's own contradiction). v5 seeded its failure-path fixture as apr_seed_launch_1 (campaign-launch) while giving campaign-launch no ledger row, so the gate refused it outright and the provider-failure path AC-5 and the QA script depend on was unreachable through the gate it had just built. CORRECTED: the seed now carries FOUR ledger rows — campaign-status autonomous (6/6/0/0), budget-change approval-required, campaign-launch approval-required, new-geography pinned shadow — and creative-refresh alone carries no row, so the fail-closed no-evidence case is still demonstrated from real data on a real roster class rather than on the write-failure fixture. Both pending fixtures are then genuinely approvable, which is what the 'either ordering consumes exactly one item' arithmetic needs.

THE BAND IS WIRED, NOT ASSUMED. v5 listed maturity as an argument validateIntent takes and no route computes it, so in production the comparison was against undefined and failed open. CORRECTED: both issuance routes compute maturity with the maturityFor/policyBand pair the repo already uses in GET /v1/metrics (src/api/routes.js:16/19, :157-158) and pass it; and validateIntent treats a missing or non-numeric maturity as MATURITY_BAND_BLOCKED, because a check that cannot read its input must not pass. The band remains the autonomy gate only — a human approval is the alternative authority for a class that has not earned autonomy (TR-7 read with TR-19) — and both directions are pinned by a test.

IDEMPOTENCY IS ATOMIC AND KEYED ON THE LOGICAL ACTION. v5's executor did getByNonce then write, which is check-then-act, and the approve route minted a fresh random nonce on every call, so a second tab or a retried POST of the same approval row produced two distinct nonces and wrote twice. CORRECTED in two parts. (1) The executor's dedupe uses the primitive the repo already ships: repositories.idempotency.claim(tenantId, nonce, 'executor') before the provider write, so exactly one caller reaches the provider and a loser reads back the winner's action_records row and returns its receipt with executed:false. The claim is RELEASED on a provider refusal (the repository already exposes that at :158) so a retry is a genuine retry, which is what v5 promised and could not deliver. (2) issueCapability takes an optional nonceSeed, and the approve route passes `apr:${approval_id}`, so two approves of the same row mint the SAME nonce and collapse onto the first receipt instead of writing twice. The executor's read of action_records still runs first, so a duplicate returns its receipt even while a kill switch is active.

MICRO-LIMITS SIT ABOVE EVERY SEEDED ACTION. v5 set budget-change's limit to 250_000_000 micros (₹250) — derived from, and then set below, the seed's own stated ₹300 downside (scripts/seed.js:182) — and never pinned the seeded intent's delta_micros, so the demo success path could fail MICRO_LIMIT_EXCEEDED. CORRECTED: the seed pins apr_seed_budget_1's stored intent constraints.delta_micros to 200_000_000 (₹200, inside the limit) and apr_seed_launch_1's to 0 (campaign-launch's limit is 0), and a seed-coherence test asserts every seeded approval's delta is at or under its class limit, so the demo can never be seeded into a gate it cannot pass.

RECONCILIATION IS SCOPED TO WRITES THAT CAN BE READ BACK. createDraft has no counterpart in READ_METHODS (src/integrations/meta_ads/index.js:41-46), so v5's 're-read through the read interface' step had nothing to re-read for a launch write. CORRECTED: the ACTION_METHOD contract marks each write with its read counterpart, and a write with none is documented and tested as reconciliation:'unknown' by contract rather than left to fail or to be quietly reported as reconciled.

v5's four earlier corrections are kept because they are right and I re-checked them: the executor owns the durable nonce dedupe and runs it first, while the kernel's injected port is read-only {seen} and owns REPLAYED_NONCE in isolation; the QA script runs the idempotency step before the guardian step so no step needs a live write under a freeze; the reset step is in-place (`npm run sdlc:seed -- --reset-approvals`) because the harness owns the boot (config.yml env.boot) and src/index.js holds the SQLite handle for the process lifetime, so unlinking data/app.db would leave the server on a deleted inode; and the seed carries exactly two pending fixtures with fixed ids and distinct classes.

ALSO CARRIED from v5: ACTION_CLASSES derived from DECISION_CLASSES (src/domain/decisions.js:21-26 freezes budget-change, campaign-status, creative-refresh, campaign-launch) with new-geography as the single explicit policy-only extension; the read path for a global-scope kill switch, with no '' sentinel, so repositories.js:4's every-query-binds-tenant_id contract keeps holding; pending-vs-lapsed as a read-time predicate so an aged row can never render in both the queue and the lapsed section; the five-state loading/error/partial early-returns in approvals() preserved verbatim so test/web/pages.test.js:55-63's /stale|await|Expired|provisional/i assertion still has something to match on an empty database; expiry clamped to min(ttlMs, approval.expires_at); docs/ui.md:35's typing-free explicit confirm, so approve is two-step; and src/web/client.js's false '<100 lines' header comment corrected to the real constraint.

A pending card whose class posture is shadow or no-evidence renders its approve button DISABLED with the same rule wording the kernel enforces, so the page can never invite an action the gate refuses. This is unreachable on the seed after the fixture fix above, which is exactly why it needs a test rather than a hope.

files.change: Pure domain module, no IO. ACTION_CLASSES is DERIVED from DECISION_CLASSES imported from src/domain/decisions.js and extended by exactly one explicit policy-only entry, new-geography; each class carries {microLimitMicros, requiredMaturityBand} and POLICY_ONLY_CLASSES is exported so a caller can label those rows policy-only rather than journal-representable. Limits in integer micros (TR-1): budget-change microLimitMicros 250_000_000 / requiredMaturityBand 'protective'; campaign-launch 0 / 'protective'; creative-refresh 0 / 'moderate'; campaign-status 0 / 'emergency-only' (a status flip moves no money and is the canonical emergency-band action, so the seeded demo's immature store does not by itself make the class unauthonomous); new-geography 0 / 'strategic'. validateIntent(intent, {nowIso, trust, approval, maturity}) -> {ok,intent}|{ok:false,error} is the ONLY place a capability can be minted, so it is where the trust gate lives. Order of its checks, and the order is the contract: (1) MALFORMED_INTENT — the action class is not on the roster; (2) AUTONOMY_NOT_EARNED — resolve the posture from the injected `trust` value ('autonomous-under-micro-limits' | 'approval-required' | 'shadow' | 'no-evidence'): shadow and no-evidence are refused outright even with a valid approval, and approval-required is refused unless `approval` is a row for the same tenant and action class whose status is 'pending' and whose expires_at is in the future; a mismatched, terminal or expired approval is AUTONOMY_NOT_EARNED too, with details naming which of the three failed; (3) MICRO_LIMIT_EXCEEDED — constraints.delta_micros exceeds the class limit, checked as a safe non-negative integer and never coerced from a float or a numeric string; (4) MATURITY_BAND_BLOCKED — AUTONOMOUS PATH ONLY, and FAIL CLOSED: an undefined, null or non-numeric `maturity` is blocked, never treated as 'no band to check', because a check that cannot read its input must not pass. The band is the autonomy gate and a human approval is the alternative authority for a class that has not earned autonomy (TR-7 read with TR-19): an approval-required class with a valid approval is governed by the human plus the micro-limit, and its band still stops it from ever becoming autonomous. Both directions are stated in the doc comment and pinned by a test. issueCapability(validated, {secret, policyVersion, ttlMs, nowIso, expiresAtCap, nonceSeed}) — the first argument is the {ok, intent} object validateIntent returns, NOT a bare intent, so a caller cannot sign something the kernel did not clear; it throws or rejects on anything else. Signs with node:crypto createHmac and timingSafeEqual and returns {tenant, resource, action, constraints, expiry, nonce, policy_version} plus a cap_-prefixed id; expiry is min(now+ttlMs, expiresAtCap) when a cap is passed, so a capability minted from an approval can never outlive it. When nonceSeed is given the nonce is derived deterministically from it (HMAC of seed+tenant+action+resource under the signing secret, hex-truncated), so two issuances of the SAME logical action collapse onto one nonce; without a seed the nonce is random. validateCapability(capability, {secret, nowIso, killSwitches, nonces}) -> {ok,capability}|{ok:false,error} with codes MALFORMED_CAPABILITY, BAD_SIGNATURE, EXPIRED_CAPABILITY, REPLAYED_NONCE, OVER_SCOPE (details name the violated constraint), KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE, MICRO_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, MATURITY_BAND_BLOCKED. Both ports are INJECTED and non-mutating: killSwitches {isActive(scope, scopeId)}, nonces {seen(nonce)} — seen, not claim; claiming a nonce is the executor's job, and this module must never reserve one. validateCapability deliberately does NOT consult trust: the capability is signed authority, and re-gating it against live ledger state at execution time would let a later ledger edit retroactively invalidate an issued capability. Imports no driver, provider, repository, sqlite or process.env; the secret arrives as an argument only.
files.why: One minter is the answer to the recorded rejection, and making issueCapability take validateIntent's return value is what turns that from a claim into a type the routes cannot get wrong. Deriving ACTION_CLASSES from DECISION_CLASSES is what stops this becoming the two-sources-of-truth failure src/domain/decisions.js:1-8 exists to prevent. One owner per nonce check is what makes AC-1 and AC-2 simultaneously satisfiable.

files.change: Pure. scoreFor(row) over a stored ledger row {evaluated, correct, needless, downside_penalties} and postureFor(actionClass, row) -> 'autonomous-under-micro-limits' | 'approval-required' | 'shadow' | 'no-evidence', with documented thresholds (autonomous requires >= 3 evaluated for that class, precision >= 0.90 and false-intervention rate <= 0.05), a pinned flag forcing shadow regardless of score, and the distinct value 'no-evidence' for a class with no row at all (TR-24, fail closed). files.why: TR-19 needs a per-class number, and one pure function over one stored ledger is what keeps the posture table and the gate on the same source. Naming the callers explicitly is the fix for the exact contradiction the rejection cited.

files.change: createExecutor({repositories, provider, kernel, auditClock}). The only module that calls a provider WRITE_METHOD. Deliberately takes NO trust parameter: the trust gate is at issuance (src/policy/kernel.js validateIntent) and this module's doc comment says so and points at it, so the two are not confused again. execute(capability, {actor}) runs its checks in THIS order, and the order is the contract: (1) DURABLE DEDUPE FIRST, in two sub-steps that together close the race v5 left open — (1a) read action_records by nonce and, if a receipt already exists, return {executed:false, receipt_id, reconciliation} immediately without validating through the kernel and without calling the provider; (1b) ATOMIC CLAIM: repositories.idempotency.claim(tenantId, nonce, 'executor') before any provider call, so of two racing deliveries exactly one proceeds; a false return means another caller won, so wait for its action_records row and return that winner's {executed:false, receipt_id, reconciliation} with no provider call. A duplicate delivery performs no mutation, so it returns its receipt even while a kill switch is active — stated in the doc comment so no one 'fixes' it into a 409. (2) kernel validateCapability, which is where KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE and the signature/expiry/scope rejections happen. (3) resolve the write method from the capability's SIGNED action through the contract module's ACTION_METHOD map (never from anything the caller passes at execute time) and call it on the injected provider. (4) re-read provider state through the read counterpart named for that write in the contract and classify drift (reported differs from applied; source 'manual'|'platform'|'third-party' as the provider reports it, 'none' when they agree); a write with NO read counterpart — createDraft — returns reconciliation:'unknown' by contract rather than inventing a value or reporting a reconciliation it cannot compute, and this is documented on the contract, not only in the executor. (5) append the action_records receipt and an audit event carrying actor and capability id, then RELEASE the claim; return {executed:true, receipt_id, requested, reported, reconciliation, drift}. A provider refusal (ok:false) releases the claim via the repository's release (src/data/repositories.js:158), returns {executed:false, error, reconciliation:'unknown'}, writes NO action_records row, and leaves the caller's approval pending, so a retry is a genuine retry rather than a silently swallowed claim. The provider is injected per request; the executor never constructs one.
files.why: Durable nonce state lives in the repository the executor already writes, not in the per-request fake (src/api/routes.js builds a new one per request, so a fake-side dedupe could not survive the two deliveries AC-2 describes). Using the repo's own claim primitive rather than get-then-act is what makes the guarantee hold under two racing requests, and the release-on-refusal is what keeps 'a retry is a genuine retry' true.

The autonomy gate's placement at issuance rather than execution is a design argument, not a spec quotation: a signed capability is authority, and re-gating it on live ledger state at execution time would let a later ledger edit retroactively invalidate a capability a human already approved. It is pinned by a test in both directions, but a reviewer who disagrees should change the executor and that test together, deliberately.

work_order.debate_summary: The critique was right about the diagnosis and right about four things that would have shipped broken, so most of it is folded in. I want to be specific about the disagreement, because the proposal and the critique were not equally right and neither was tidy. The critique's two BLOCKING findings are real and I confirmed both against v5's own text rather than taking them on trust. First: v5 claimed validateIntent was the only place a capability could be minted, and then specified the approve route resolving the posture itself, refusing only 'not shadow', and calling issueCapability directly — so the gate had two owners and the one that escaped was the human-approval path, the money-moving one, which skipped the micro-limit, the band and the no-evidence refusal. That is the exact defect the previous rejection was about, one layer down: v4 was caught shipping a ledger enforced by nothing, and v5 was caught shipping a gate the money path walked around. The fix is structural rather than textual — a shared issuance helper both routes call, plus issueCapability taking validateIntent's return object so a route cannot sign an unvalidated intent even by accident, plus a boundary test that pins the call sites. Second: v5 seeded its failure-path fixture as campaign-launch with no ledger row, which its own gate refuses outright, so AC-5's 502 reconciliation panel and the QA step that produces it were unreachable through the gate it had just built. One seeded ledger row fixes it, and it also lets me keep the no-evidence demonstration on creative-refresh where it costs nothing. I took the three MAJOR findings too: the band gate was wired to nothing and failed open on an undefined maturity (the fix reuses maturityFor/policyBand, already imported at routes.js:16/19 — one line of reuse, not new machinery), and validateIntent now fails closed on an unreadable input; budget-change's 250,000,000 limit sat below the seed's own 300,000,000 figure at scripts/seed.js:182 with the fixture's delta never pinned, which could break the demo's own success path; and the dedupe was get-then-act while the repo already ships the single-winner primitive the plan never used. I took the MINOR finding on createDraft having no read counterpart, and folded it as a contract property with a test rather than a comment. I also took the edge case the proposal missed entirely — a pending card whose class is shadow renders a live Approve button the gate will refuse — because the page and the gate must not disagree in the same way the plan contradicted itself twice. What I REJECTED, explicitly: the critique's suggestion to give some class a requiredMaturityBand above the seeded store's band 'so the gate is demonstrably live'. campaign-status is the only class the seed calibrates autonomous, so raising its band makes the autonomous path fail MATURITY_BAND_BLOCKED and IAC-4's live case unobservable. The honest move is to wire the gate correctly and say in residual_risks that the demo does not exercise it, which I have done; a demo that demonstrates itself by refusing to run is not a demonstration. I also rejected its alternative of dropping MATURITY_BAND_BLOCKED entirely — TR-7 is in this issue's coverage list, and a roster the kernel does not gate is the same display-only defect one field over. I rejected its framing of the idempotency finding as a demand to re-key on approval id: that is the right instinct for the approval path and I folded it in as a deterministic nonce seed, but as a REPLACEMENT for the nonce it would break AC-2, whose duplicate is the same capability posted twice with no approval in the request at all. The two are complementary and the work order now carries both. Two more of its edge cases I declined to turn into design changes: the in-flight freeze straddle is unreachable while the fake's writes are synchronous and belongs with the real write path, and the unicode round-trip is already covered by the escaped-copy assertion, which I extended to include the two-step confirm state rather than treating as a new gap. I did not simply accept the critique's severity ordering either: the two blocking findings are load-bearing for the recorded rejection, the band and idempotency findings are real but do not defeat a criterion on their own, and the createDraft one is a contract statement. Separately, BOTH documents missed something and I am recording it rather than leaving it to a reviewer: v5's AC-2 says 'qa_script step 7' for the idempotency step and AC-5 says 'steps 5-6' for the two approvals, but the script has nine steps and those are steps 8 and 6-7 — the same unrenumbered-pointer error v3 was corrected for, reappearing after the script grew. I have removed the numeric pointers from the acceptance criteria entirely and named each step by its content, so a future edit to the script cannot silently invalidate a criterion. The proposal's own unknowns stay unresolved and I have not dressed them up: the capability-issuance surface is unauthenticated, the drift source is fake-only, and the live Meta mutation surface is unread by design.

validated_work_order.root_cause: There is no write path to gate, and no stored decision to gate it on. Nothing between an ActionIntent and a provider write exists, so TR-2, TR-3, TR-4, TR-5, TR-19 and TR-24 have no code to hold them; and because the approvals page reads an event type nothing writes and a hardcoded posture constant, a trust ledger built on those foundations would be a rendered table that no write path ever consults — the exact 'looks finished while shipping' shape the recorded review rejected. Four secondary defects would each have shipped silently on top of that: the v5 gate's maturity-band rule had no value anywhere to read it from, the v5 nonce was minted per issuance so a retried approve could write twice, the global kill switch had no stated scope_id so a second trigger would append rather than update, and the approvals empty branch was going to be dropped by a rewrite whose own QA script reaches it on every run.
validated_work_order.approach:
Build the write path as four new modules plus one composition point, on the repo's existing patterns. v5's central design decision is right and I kept it: the recorded review is correct that autonomy within micro-limits is in scope (the issue defers only autonomy BEYOND micro-limits, and IAC-4's verb is 'executes'), so the gate is IMPLEMENTED at kernel.validateIntent rather than deferred, a class whose posture is not autonomous and which has no approval row cannot produce a capability at all, and AUTONOMY_NOT_EARNED is a named code asserted both as a unit and over HTTP.

WHAT I FIXED FROM THE CRITIQUE (I re-checked every one against the file and line it cited; nine of eleven findings held and are folded in below, and the two parts I reject are named in debate_summary rather than dropped).

1. MATURITY HAD NO SOURCE. v5's validateIntent took {nowIso, posture, approval} yet the same sentence made the rule 'within the class micro-limit and maturity band', and MATURITY_BAND_BLOCKED was a named code with a test case. Nothing anywhere supplied a maturity. FIXED: `maturity` is now an explicit option of validateIntent, and files[9] names its source in the repo's own terms — the tenant's raw-event data-through age through maturityFor/policyBand, the same computation GET /v1/metrics already performs at src/api/routes.js:173-175, reused rather than invented. On seed data every event is stamped occurredAt() (scripts/seed.js:72,84,96), so data-through age is ~0h, maturityFor(0) is 0 and policyBand is 'emergency-only'; the seeded classes carry requiredMaturityBand 'emergency-only' so seed data is admitted, and a test pins AC-4's exact request body as ADMITTED rather than leaving it to a reading. v5's assumption that 'maturity is ~0.06 because seed decisions are six hours old' was wrong twice over — 0.06 is one decision's age (scripts/seed.js:256) and the other two are 150h (maturityFor(150) = 1.0) — so the assumption is rewritten around the source that actually exists.

2. EXACTLY-ONCE WAS PER NONCE, NOT PER APPROVAL. v5 minted a fresh nonce inside issueCapability on every call, so a lost response after the provider applied the write leaves the row pending and a second click writes again. FIXED: on the approve path the nonce is DERIVED from the approval — 'apr_' + approvalId — so any redelivery of that approval hits the same action_records.nonce; and POST /v1/approvals/:id/approve looks that receipt up BEFORE its status check, returning 200 {executed:false, receipt_id} rather than the 409 a retry would otherwise get. This is the server-side invariant the critique's server-enforced `confirm` (finding 7) also asked for, and it closes the second-browser-tab race that the per-tab client guard never could. On the autonomous path the nonce stays freshly minted per issuance, which is correct: there is no approval identity to bind it to.

3. THE CHOKE-POINT ARGUMENT WAS STATED FALSELY. v5's files[0].why said validateIntent is 'the choke point both capability-issuing routes already call'; no such route exists, this change creates both. FIXED: files[0] now says both routes call it because this change wires them, and states plainly that POST /v1/actions/execute is a bearer-token surface whose only control is the signature — the trust ledger gates issuance, not execution, by design. I keep that asymmetry (see debate_summary). But the critique found a real hole next to it: the envelope carries `tenant`, resolveTenantId derives one from the request, and nothing required them to match, so a cross-tenant write was expressible. FIXED: /v1/actions/execute refuses an envelope whose tenant differs from the resolved tenant with 409 TENANT_MISMATCH, and the executor's nonce lookups become tenant-qualified (item 4).

4. THE GLOBAL KILL SWITCH HAD NO scope_id. v5's PK(tenant_id, scope, scope_id) permits NULL, SQLite never matches a NULL in an ON CONFLICT target, so a second spend-spike would append a second active row that the re-enable would not clear — the freeze would survive forever and AC-3's 'banner clears only after explicit re-enable' would fail. FIXED: scope_id is NOT NULL, the global-scope row carries the literal tenant_id as its scope_id so the key is (tenant_id,'global',tenant_id) and ON CONFLICT always matches, reEnable takes the full key, and a new guardian test freezes, re-enables, re-triggers the SAME kind and asserts exactly one active row.

5. THE APPROVALS EMPTY BRANCH WAS GOING TO BE DROPPED. I confirmed it exists at src/web/pages.js:836-843, is pinned by docs/ui.md:104 ('emptiness reads as healthy'), and is reached whenever pending.length === 0 under the DERIVED state — which is exactly the state v5's own qa_script leaves behind, since it approves one fixture and rejects the other. No test would have gone red: pages.test.js:45 asserts only the posture heading, and the override test at :48-68 covers loading, partial and error only. FIXED: the empty branch joins the PRESERVE VERBATIM list, and a new test asserts that a tenant with zero pending approvals renders both [data-testid=approvals-empty] and the posture table through the derived state rather than a ?state= override.

6. THE TR-2 TEST COULD NOT CATCH THE DEFECT IT EXISTS FOR. v5 allowedlisted src/api/routes.js for the string POLICY_SIGNING_SECRET, but a hardcoded default constant in routes.js mentions no env var and passes while producing exactly the live-key state files[4] exists to prevent. FIXED: the assertion is on the VALUE — the dev-default literal appears in exactly one file under src/, and that file is src/index.js; routes.js is asserted to import no signing constant from src/policy/.

7. CLIENT BEHAVIOUR HAD NO EXECUTABLE COVERAGE. The two-step confirm and the in-flight guard were asserted as markup, which is identical whether or not either is wired, and the repo has no DOM harness. FIXED the part that matters and is cheap: the confirm becomes a SERVER invariant — POST /v1/approvals/:id/approve requires a `confirm` field and returns 400 CONFIRM_REQUIRED without it, asserted over HTTP — which also survives the lost-response retry. I decline to add a DOM harness (out of proportion for one vanilla IIFE); the rest of client.js is covered by qa_script only and residual_risks says so plainly rather than implying coverage that does not exist.

8. NONCE UNIQUENESS WAS NOT TENANT-BOUND. `nonce UNIQUE` is global while every other column is per-tenant, getByNonce/seen took no tenant, and this contradicts src/data/repositories.js:4. FIXED: UNIQUE(tenant_id, nonce) on both tables, getByNonce(tenantId, nonce) and seen(tenantId, nonce), and a tenant-isolation case proving a second tenant's delivery of the same nonce string is not deduped against the first tenant's receipt.

9. FOUR CITATIONS WERE WRONG. src/web/client.js is 154 lines, not 130, so v5's 'already exceeded at 130' understated it; the seed console.log is scripts/seed.js:473-477 and alreadySeeded is the :465-466 return predicate, which v5 swapped; the buildApp count is ten outside routes.js, nine of them tests. All are corrected here. They changed no design and cost nothing but reviewer trust.

10. THE RESET COMMAND COULD FAIL WITH SQLITE_BUSY. src/data/db.js:280 opens with no PRAGMA busy_timeout, so the seed process writing while the server holds the lock fails immediately rather than waiting — and that command is the single point every browser criterion hangs off. FIXED: openDatabase sets `PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000`, which covers both connections and both processes, and qa_script step 2 states the expected failure text so a busy lock is distinguishable from an empty queue.

11. TWO CRITERIA WERE MISCLASSIFIED. 'The banner is on all five pages' has no curl equivalent. FIXED: AC-3 is now browser and a new AC-6 carries the curl half (409, re-enable refused without an actor, banner returns on re-trigger); AC-4 stays api because the enforced gate is its substantive half, and a new AC-7 carries the posture table as browser.

I ALSO FIXED WHAT NEITHER PLAN NOR CRITIQUE CAUGHT: a reason that is whitespace-only or a non-string must not pass a naive `!reason` check — 400 REASON_REQUIRED covers trimmed-empty and non-string, asserted over HTTP, since the reason is operator-supplied text that the client also echoes into the toast.

Everything else in v5 stands and I re-verified it against the code: the fake provider's typed WRITE_METHODS and extended failure injection, the per-request provider built from ?meta_error exactly as src/api/routes.js:103 does for pages (constructor takes only {failureMode}, which is why v4's stateStore option would have been a silent no-op), the pending-vs-lapsed read-time predicate, ACTION_CLASSES derived from DECISION_CLASSES (src/domain/decisions.js:21-26) with new-geography as the one explicit policy-only extension, src/index.js composing the signing secret with one startup warning, the loading/error/partial early-returns surviving verbatim, and no live mutation path at all (live.js gains no write method; the process holds no ad credentials). The triage finding stays fixed by omission: this work order names no .sdlc/** path, which `node .sdlc/bin/check-forbidden.mjs --file plan/proposal.json` confirms over the v5 file set ('no forbidden paths (23 checked)'), and the QA documentation content is delivered inside qa_script instead.

risks: Highest-risk slice in the project: money movement, auth-equivalent capabilities, credential isolation and kill switches. test/executor/credential-isolation.test.js is the static import-boundary check TR-2 asks for and is a required part of this work order, not a nice-to-have — and it is now asserted on the signing literal's location rather than on a variable name, so it can actually fail.

The autonomy gate makes an executive call about what may execute without a human. If validateIntent admits something it should not, a write happens with no approval. It therefore fails closed on every ambiguous input — an unknown class, a missing or unrecognised posture, a malformed approval row, and a missing maturity are all refusals, not defaults — and the refusal is a named code, not a throw.

POST /v1/actions/execute is a bearer-token surface: the trust ledger gates ISSUANCE and never execution, by design, because a signed capability is the attestation and a second owner for one check would let a trust-row edit retroactively invalidate a correctly issued capability. Its only controls are signature, expiry, scope, tenant and the kill switch. With the signing secret defaulting to a public dev constant, that surface is forgeable by anyone holding the source. This is bounded today only by the fact that the only writable provider is the in-memory fake; it is the first thing to revisit when a live write path lands, and residual_risks says so.

This slice adds no real mutation path: live.js gains no write method and the process holds no ad credentials. That is deliberate, and it means an approved budget change is NOT visible on a later dashboard load — the receipt's reconciliation record is the evidence, not the campaign table. QA should not expect / to change after an approval.

The capability signing secret defaults to a dev-only value in every environment that exists, because project.md records no deployment. The mitigation is that the default is named, warned about once at startup, overridable via POLICY_SIGNING_SECRET, and confined to one file by an executable test — not that it is removed, which would leave CI and browser QA unable to verify a signature deterministically.

Migration 006 must stay additive and idempotent: every statement is CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS and the five existing migrations are untouched, because a runner may already hold a database from #19 through #21. The number is 006 and not 005 because 005_opportunity_experiment_tables is already in the array at src/data/db.js:223.

Two schema-level constraints are load-bearing and read as ordinary: UNIQUE(tenant_id, nonce) rather than a global nonce, and a NOT NULL scope_id. Both exist because of SQLite behaviours that no reviewer reads off the schema at a glance — NULLs are distinct in a rowid PRIMARY KEY, so an ON CONFLICT target with a NULL scope_id never matches and a re-enable can never clear the freeze. The guardian test that triggers the same kind twice is what holds both honest.

Approvals rows are mutable by design while action_records and guardian_incidents are append-only with storage triggers; a re-enable therefore records on kill_switches and audit_events and never updates an incident. An implementer who reaches for UPDATE on an incident breaks TR-20. resetSeededFixtures is a deliberate, documented exception on the mutable approvals table and touches only the four seeded ids.

alternatives_considered.approach: Defer autonomous execution within micro-limits (the recorded review's option (b)): add it to out_of_scope and rewrite AC-4 to verify only the posture table
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The issue's out_of_scope defers only 'Autonomous strategic actions BEYOND micro-limits', so micro-limit autonomy is in scope, and IAC-4's verb is 'executes'. The review's own complaint was that a display-only check passes on a plan where the ledger is inert; a deferral would have reproduced the same gap with a note attached. A deferral would also leave a trust ledger with no reader for a later slice to rediscover.

alternatives_considered.approach: Move the posture check into the executor as well as at issuance, so /v1/actions/execute is also gated on the ledger
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Two owners for one check, and the second is wrong: a trust row edited between issuance and execution would retroactively invalidate a correctly signed capability, so a legitimate write would fail for a reason the signer cannot see. validateIntent is the single gate and a signed capability is the attestation; the executor re-checks only what can change underneath a capability — signature, expiry, scope, tenant, kill switch. The asymmetry is accepted and stated in files[9] and in risks rather than papered over, because the honest version of this design is that the execute surface is a bearer-token surface.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep a freshly minted nonce per issuance and instead make the client disable the approve button until a response arrives
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The guard is per-tab and client-side, so a second tab or a lost response still writes twice, and the failing case is precisely the one where the operator most needs to retry. Deriving the nonce from the approval and looking the receipt up before the status check makes the server idempotent, which is the only place this is actually true.

alternatives_considered.approach: Let validateIntent read the approvals and raw-events repositories directly instead of taking the approval row and maturity as arguments
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It would make the policy kernel impure and break the import-boundary test in test/executor/credential-isolation.test.js — the kernel exists to be a deterministic pure function. It would also make the maturity SOURCE implicit, which is the defect this work order fixes: the source is named in one place, the route, and pinned by a test.

alternatives_considered.approach: A single combined src/policy/safety.js holding kernel, trust, guardian and executor
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It would put the provider write call in the same file as the policy rules and the HMAC secret's reach, which is precisely the boundary TR-2 requires be provable with a static import check

alternatives_considered.approach: JWT library (jose) for capability signing
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: A new runtime dependency for what node:crypto's createHmac with timingSafeEqual does in a few lines; conventions require stdlib first with a one-line justification and there is none to give

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep one pending approval fixture and rewrite AC-5 plus the script to approve the same still-pending item twice
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It makes a browser criterion depend on a subtle two-step order on one item, and a QA run that succeeds on the first click leaves nothing to fail on the second. Two distinct fixtures satisfy both orderings and give the posture table a second calibrated row for free.

alternatives_considered.approach: Nonce idempotency held in the fake provider, as an earlier plan had it
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The provider is constructed per request (src/api/routes.js:103), so it holds no state across the two deliveries AC-2 describes; durable dedupe on action_records.nonce in the executor is the only place it can hold

alternatives_considered.approach: Give the kernel a mutating {claim(nonce)} port and let it reject a replay before the executor's action_records lookup
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: This contradicts AC-2: the second delivery would get an error envelope instead of the original receipt, and the kernel has no way to produce a receipt_id. The executor dedupes first, the kernel's port stays read-only {seen}, and both criteria hold.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep a '' sentinel tenant_id for the global kill switch and give isActive a special two-scope read
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It needs a deliberate exception to the module contract at src/data/repositories.js:4 ('Every query binds tenant_id, so isolation holds on every path'), and a reader who misses the exception silently loses the global freeze. A global-scope row carrying a real tenant_id is read by the same union query with no exception at all.

assumptions: The QA harness owns the server boot (.sdlc/config.yml:107 env.boot = npm run sdlc:serve) and can run `npm run sdlc:seed -- --reset-approvals` against the same ./data/app.db the running server has open. The script entry is `node scripts/seed.js`, so npm passes the flag through as argv. If the harness cannot pass extra argv, the same reset is reachable as `node scripts/seed.js --reset-approvals`; either way it must not unlink the database file or restart the server. This is the assumption every browser criterion depends on and it is the one thing I could not verify from the code. What the code DOES settle, unlike the prior plan's version of this assumption: the database is opened with no busy timeout, so this slice adds PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000 and qa_script step 2 states the expected busy-error text so a lock is distinguishable from an empty queue.

Maturity for the gate is the tenant's raw-event data-through age, computed through the repo's own maturityFor and policyBand — the same computation GET /v1/metrics performs at src/api/routes.js:173-175. On seed data every raw event is stamped occurredAt() (scripts/seed.js:72,84,96), so the age is ~0h, maturityFor(0) is 0 and the band is 'emergency-only'; the seeded classes carry requiredMaturityBand 'emergency-only' so seed data is admitted. This replaces the previous plan's claim that maturity is ~0.06 because the seed decisions are six hours old, which was wrong twice: 0.06 is one decision's age and the other two seeded decisions are 150h, which reads as maturity 1.0. The kernel's band-rejection cases use explicit maturity fixtures, and a test asserts AC-4's exact request body is ADMITTED on seed data, so the value is pinned by an assertion rather than by a reading of this sentence.

The approve path supplies the approval row it is executing to validateIntent, so a non-autonomous class is admitted by an explicit human approval and refused without one. I read IAC-4's 'new-geography marked shadow or approval' as sanctioning exactly this: shadow means never autonomous, approval means a human may still say yes.

An approval is created by strategy code in a later slice; this slice only decides, executes and records, so the seed and the tests are the only approval writers. This is also why nothing in this change can detect two pending approvals for the same resource — no component here proposes, so the duplicate case is deferred rather than solved.

A signed capability is valid on its own authority for its whole lifetime and is not re-checked against the trust ledger at execute time (see alternatives_considered for why a second owner is worse). One consequence I am choosing rather than discovering: a capability issued before a freeze and executed after the re-enable is admitted, because validateCapability sees an inactive switch. That is recorded in residual_risks rather than left to be found.
unknowns: The exact Graph mutation endpoints and field names a live write would use. Deliberately untouched: live.js gains no write method, so no write contract beyond the typed shapes is committed to here.

How a real provider reports drift source. The fake reports it from simulateDrift and the executor classifies whatever the provider names; against a live provider this needs a platform-side signal this slice does not have.

Whether the QA harness runs each qa_script step against the same server process. Every step is written to be safe either way — the reset is in-place and no step boots or kills the server — but if steps are split across processes, the last step's freeze outlives the process and the next run's reset still clears it.
Whether a human will want a third posture between 'shadow' and 'approval-required' (for example shadow-but-overridable). TR-19 and IAC-4 only name the two, so I implemented the two.

Whether the approval-derived nonce scheme survives a later slice where a single approved intent legitimately needs more than one provider write (for example updateBudget then setCampaignStatus). The scheme is correct for one-write-per-approval, which is all this slice has; a multi-step action would need a sub-nonce and that is a design question for the slice that first needs it.
residual_risks: QA reads these first. (1) POST /v1/actions/execute is a bearer-token surface whose only control is the signing secret, and the secret has a public dev default — a capability forged offline is accepted without the trust ledger ever being consulted, and a cross-tenant envelope is refused only because this work order adds the TENANT_MISMATCH check. (2) The two-step confirm and the retry safety were moved to the server precisely because the repo has no DOM harness; the REST of client.js — the in-flight guard, the toast fill, the pending-count decrement, the reason input surviving a failure — has NO executable coverage and is verified by qa_script steps 6-7 only. Read those assertions as human observation, not as a regression net. (3) The signing secret's dev default is live wherever POLICY_SIGNING_SECRET is unset, which today is everywhere; the blast radius is bounded only by the fact that the only writable provider is the in-memory fake. (4) .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md and environment.md are NOT updated by this work order — the triage finding is correct that a ticket branch may not touch them, and qa_script is a substitute, not a replacement. They stay stale about the new data-testids, the new /v1 routes and the --reset-approvals re-run contract until the Librarian's branch is refreshed. (5) A capability issued before a freeze and executed after the re-enable is admitted, because validateCapability sees an inactive switch; nothing records that the capability predates the freeze. (6) Two pending approvals for the same action_class and resource both execute — correct for this slice, since nothing here proposes, and asserted so a future dedupe is deliberate. (7) Maturity bands mean no action class requiring above 0.35 maturity is autonomous in the seeded demo, so the kernel tests assert band rejection with explicit maturity fixtures rather than the live clock, and a change to the band thresholds would not be caught by that suite. (8) The ?meta_error simulation is a URL-level switch with no on-page indication: a bookmarked /approvals?meta_error=quota makes every approval fail silently with no way to clear it from the page. Pre-existing on /, unchanged here, filed in out_of_scope. (9) With buildApp's policyConfig optional, the dev-default secret applies inside every existing test, so signature tests pass against a secret no test controls. (10) The five-state shells, the 404 envelope for unknown /v1 paths and the fake provider's cross-request statelessness are contracts this change edits or extends; test/web/approvals.test.js, test/api/*.test.js and test/integrations/meta_ads.test.js cover them explicitly, so read those assertions as the regression net rather than trusting this description.
validated_work_order.confidence_rationale: The root cause is verified and not in doubt — there is no src/policy/, no src/executor/, no guardian, and the approvals page is exactly the empty static shell both prior plans describe, so the design rests on code I read rather than on a guess. All five split criteria (IAC-1..IAC-5) are carried, the recorded rejection is answered by implementing the gate rather than by deferring it, and the recorded triage finding is fixed by omission in a way a command verifies rather than argues. I am below the previous plan's 82, and deliberately so: I re-checked every load-bearing claim in the critique against the file and line it cited, and nine of eleven held. That two consecutive rounds each contained two blocking defects of exactly the kind that a passing unit test will not catch — a gate rule with no input, a nonce with no identity behind it, an upsert that cannot match its own row — is itself evidence about how much of a plan like this can be trusted from paper. What they cost is now specifiable rather than probable, which is most of why I am at 78 rather than lower. What would move it up: an implementer writing test/policy/kernel.test.js and test/api/approvals.test.js FIRST and seeing the maturity input, the approval-derived nonce and the receipt-before-status ordering hold together — that intersection is the one place the autonomy path, the approval path and idempotency all meet, and it is the place a wrong reading shows up fastest. What would move it down, and it is not far: QA discovering it cannot pass --reset-approvals against the live server's open handle, since every browser criterion hangs off that one command. The busy-timeout finding sharpened that rather than reassuring me — the previous plan called this assumption unverifiable when part of it was in fact readable, and the same over-confidence about which things are settled is what produced two of the blocking findings. If QA hits a busy lock even with the timeout, this number is too high.
validated_work_order.debate_summary: The critique was substantially right and I say so plainly: nine of its eleven findings survived my own re-check against the cited lines, including both it marked blocking, and each is folded into files[], tests[] or acceptance[] below rather than argued away. The two blocking ones are the ones that would have shipped. The maturity-band half of the autonomy gate had no value anywhere in the plan — validateIntent's signature carried no maturity, no route computed one, and the assumption's supporting number (~0.06) was the age of a single seed decision rather than anything the repo computes, while the other two seeded decisions are 150h and read as maturity 1.0. That is not a detail; it decides whether the criterion that the recorded rejection was about returns 200 or 403, from a value nobody had placed. I specified the source in the repo's own terms (the raw-event data-through computation GET /v1/metrics already performs at routes.js:173-175) and added a test that pins AC-4's exact request body as admitted on seed data, so the value is held by an assertion instead of by my reading. The second blocking finding is the one I like least as a class of defect: a nonce minted per issuance gives exactly-once per capability, not per approval, so a lost response after the provider applied the write — the case where the row is still pending and the plan's own 409 does not fire — becomes a double spend on the second click. I fixed it at the server by deriving the nonce from the approval and returning an existing receipt before the status check, which also closes the second-browser-tab race that the client guard never could. I rejected the critique's proposed alternative of testing client.js more thoroughly on grounds I half accept and half decline: the diagnosis is right that an unwired one-step button and a wired two-step button produce identical HTML, but the fix it offers (require a `confirm` field server-side) I took, while adding a DOM harness I put in out_of_scope as out of proportion for one vanilla IIFE. I also took its tenant-binding point, which was a genuine hole rather than a nuance — the envelope carries a tenant, the request derives one, and nothing required them to match, on the one write surface the gate does not cover. What I did not take from the critique is its primary suggested fix to finding 3: moving the posture check into the execute path. I keep the asymmetry, and I want to be honest that this is a disagreement rather than a resolution. The critique's own analysis concedes the one-owner argument holds — re-deriving posture at execute time would let a trust-row edit retroactively invalidate a correctly signed capability — and a surface gated only by a signature is a legitimate design for a bearer capability. What I refused to do is leave it implicit: files[9] now says in one sentence that /v1/actions/execute is a bearer-token surface the trust ledger does not and cannot gate, risks says plainly that the dev-default secret makes that surface forgeable by anyone holding the source, and tests[] asserts unsigned and tampered envelopes over HTTP rather than only as unit calls. The critique graded that finding major partly on a forged-envelope alarm; I think the alarm is real but is the price of a recorded choice, and a choice honestly stated is worth more than a plan that pretends the surface does not exist. Three findings I took as they stand because they are cheap and correct: the approvals empty branch (I confirmed it at pages.js:836-843, pinned by docs/ui.md:104, reached through the DERIVED state whenever the queue is empty — which is exactly the state this work order's own QA script leaves behind on every run, and which no existing assertion would catch); the global kill switch's undefined scope_id (SQLite never matches a NULL in an ON CONFLICT target, so a second trigger would have appended a row no re-enable could clear and AC-3 would have failed); and the missing busy timeout, which turned the single assumption this plan cannot verify from code into one that at least fails loudly and distinguishably instead of silently. The four wrong line citations — client.js is 154 not 130, the seed's console line and alreadySeeded predicate were transposed, the buildApp count is ten not nine — I corrected and otherwise disregard; none changed a design, and I note them only because a reader who found four wrong numbers will not check the rest of the file as carefully. Two things neither the plan nor the critique caught I added because I found them while verifying: a whitespace-only or non-string reason passes a naive `!reason` check, and the reason is operator text the client also echoes into the toast. One thing I softened is AC-3 and AC-4's verification surfaces, which the critique was right to call misclassified — 'the banner is on all five pages' has no curl equivalent, so the criterion is now split into a browser half and an API half (AC-3/AC-6 and AC-4/AC-7) with the enforcement and display halves stated as the same claim rather than two checks someone can satisfy independently. I also corrected the previous plan's rhetorical claim that both capability-issuing routes 'already call' validateIntent: they do not, because this change creates them, and a plan that leans on 'already' for a function it is about to wire is a plan whose choke-point argument has not been checked.
